messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar was a 41-year-old single Middle Eastern man who worked construction in the Chicago area, a job that had suited him for years because it kept him busy and away from having to talk much. He had grown up in a home where the air could change without warning. As a boy, he had witnessed repeated violence between his parents, and one scene in particular remained lodged in him with an odd, broken quality: certain moments were vivid in a way that felt almost like photographs, while large stretches of what happened before and after them were blank. He could remember the sharp angle of his mother’s face turning away, the texture of the hallway wall under his hand, the look in his father’s eyes, but when he tried to explain the sequence of events from start to finish, he found it hard to access the memory deliberately, as if the story had been cut into fragments and some pieces had simply gone missing. The parts he could see were so clear that they seemed to sit in front of him, yet the gaps made him feel uncertain and unsettled whenever he tried to put words to it.

In the years after those childhood experiences, Omar learned to move through life by watching for signs of trouble. He became intensely alert to people’s faces and body language, studying the set of a jaw, the angle of a shoulder, or a look that might signal the beginning of anger. He described feeling a strong physical reaction when something in the present reminded him of the old fear: his body would tense, his chest would tighten, and he would feel an immediate surge of alarm that seemed out of proportion to whatever was happening around him. Confrontation of any kind had become especially hard to tolerate. If a conversation looked like it might turn into disagreement, he would back away, go quiet, or leave if he could. He had come to believe that disagreement was dangerous, not because he expected every argument to become violent, but because in his experience conflict had never been safely contained. Even ordinary delays could set him on edge. When a job ran longer than expected or someone was late to meet him, he would start assuming that something bad was happening, and he found himself scanning for explanations before anyone else had even spoken.

At work, these reactions shaped the way he handled the day. On construction sites, where supervisors, inspectors, and sometimes police officers were present, the sight of authority stirred something immediate in him. He would become tense around police in particular, even when they were simply nearby or speaking with someone else. If a foreman approached with a serious expression, Omar would watch him closely and feel his stomach drop before a single word was said. In crews where tempers sometimes flared, he did his best to avoid being drawn into disagreements. He would volunteer for tasks that kept him apart from heated conversations and tried to make himself useful in ways that did not require taking sides. Over time, this had narrowed how he moved through both work and his personal life. He had fewer close relationships than he once wished for, partly because he kept distance from situations where people might argue, and partly because he often drifted off into a world of his own when he felt overwhelmed. In those moments, he could sit in a break area, stare at nothing in particular, and mentally disappear for a while. He also found himself dwelling on how he used to be before all of this, before fear became such a familiar companion. He missed the version of himself he imagined had once been easier, more open, less guarded, though he spoke about that with a kind of resignation rather than hope.

More recently, the present had become harder to manage. The police presence at a site, a tense exchange between coworkers, or even someone saying they needed to talk about the future could jolt him. Future-oriented conversations were especially difficult because they forced him into imagining what might go wrong or what he might lose. What had finally brought him to seek help was a growing sense that he could not keep absorbing these moments on his own. He was tired of feeling his body react before he had time to think, tired of measuring everyone’s face for danger, and tired of the way delays and disagreements could pull him into fear. He wanted to understand why old scenes still returned so vividly and why so much of the memory remained inaccessible except in flashes. At the same time, what frightened him most was the possibility that nothing would change and that he would continue living as if danger were always one conversation, one look, or one delay away.
